claim: Mutations in any of more than 140 genes can cause photoreceptors in a vertebrate retina to degenerate
source: Mutations in any of more than 140 genes can cause photoreceptors in a vertebrate retina to degenerate (Bramall et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bramall et al., 2010

claim: Glucose from the choroidal blood passes through the retinal pigment epithelium to the retina where photoreceptors convert it to lactate
source: In this model, glucose from the choroidal blood passes through the retinal pigment epithelium to the retina where photoreceptors convert it to lactate.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental results including metabolic flux analysis and 2-NBDG uptake experiments

claim: Photoreceptors export lactate as fuel for the retinal pigment epithelium and for neighboring Müller glial cells
source: Photoreceptors then export the lactate as fuel for the retinal pigment epithelium and for neighboring Müller glial cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lactate metabolism in RPE and MGCs, and by inference from metabolic flux studies

claim: Lactate can suppress consumption of glucose by the retinal pigment epithelium
source: We used human retinal epithelial cells to show that lactate can suppress consumption of glucose by the retinal pigment epithelium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from hfRPE cells showing reduced glucose incorporation into metabolites in the presence of lactate

claim: Suppression of glucose consumption in the retinal pigment epithelium can increase the amount of glucose that reaches the retina
source: Suppression of glucose consumption in the retinal pigment epithelium can increase the amount of glucose that reaches the retina.
evidence: Supported by transwell experiments showing increased glucose transport across RPE monolayers in the presence of lactate

claim: Retina and RPE express GLUT1
source: We used immunoblotting of mouse tissues to evaluate expression of glucose transporters (Figure 1A) and confirmed previous findings (Badr et al., 2000; Gospe et al., 2010) that retina and RPE express GLUT1.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A and confirmed by previous citations

claim: GLUT3 was detected only in brain
source: GLUT3 was detected only in brain.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A

claim: GLUT4 was detected in heart and muscle but not in the retina
source: GLUT4 was detected in heart and muscle as expected, but not in the retina.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A

claim: GLUT1 immunoreactivity overlaps with cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (MT-COX1) which identifies rod inner segments
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) of mouse retinas shows that GLUT1 immunoreactivity overlaps with cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (MT-COX1) (Figure 1C), which identifies rod inner segments by the unique elongated shape of their mitochondria (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1C and 1E

claim: GLUT1 immunoreactivity overlaps with rod arrestin
source: GLUT1 immunoreactivity also overlaps with a marker specific for rod photoreceptors, rod arrestin (Figure 1G)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1G

claim: GLUT1 immunoreactivity overlaps with GFP expressed from the rod-specific Nrl promoter
source: and it overlaps with GFP expressed from the rod-specific Nrl promoter (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H

claim: 2-NBDG fluorescence is strongest in the photoreceptor layer
source: Figure 2A shows that 2-NBDG fluorescence is strongest in the photoreceptor layer, suggesting that most of the glucose from the blood that enters a retina is taken up by photoreceptors.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 2-NBDG fluorescence is stronger in the outer retina than in the inner retina even though mouse inner retinas are vascularized
source: Surprisingly, 2-NBDG fluorescence is stronger in the outer retina than in the inner retina even though mouse inner retinas are vascularized.
evidence: Supported by imaging data from 2-NBDG gavage experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: 2-NBDG fluorescence does not overlap with Müller glial cells
source: We noted that 2-NBDG fluorescence does not overlap with MGC's, which were labeled in these experiments by transgenic expression of tdTomato (Wohl and Reh, 2016), though in rare instances there was overlap at a MGC end foot.
evidence: Supported by imaging data from 2-NBDG gavage experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: Glucose that reaches the outer retina is taken up primarily by photoreceptors
source: These results are summarized and quantified in Figure 2C. They show that glucose that reaches the outer retina is taken up primarily by photoreceptors.
evidence: Supported by quantification of 2-NBDG fluorescence shown in Figure 2C

claim: Cones become intensely fluorescent 30 min after gavage with 2-NBDG in zebrafish
source: Figure 2B shows that cones become intensely fluorescent 30 min after gavage.
evidence: Supported by imaging data from zebrafish 2-NBDG gavage experiments shown in Figure 2B

claim: Most of the glucose taken up into a retina is used to make lactic acid
source: Previous studies showed that most of the glucose taken up into a retina is used to make lactic acid (Du et al., 2016a; Krebs, 1927; Warburg et al., 1924; Medrano and Fox, 1995; Wang et al., 1997; Winkler, 1981).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The initial rate at which 13C from glucose incorporates into the intracellular pool of lactate is at least eight times faster in mRetina than in hfRPE
source: Figure 3B shows the time course of incorporation of 13C from [1,2] 13C glucose into several key metabolites. The initial rate at which 13C from glucose incorporates into the intracellular pool of lactate is at least eight times faster in mRetina than in hfRPE.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Lactate and succinate are more abundant in mRetina than in hfRPE
source: Figure 3A shows the total pmoles per μg protein of several metabolites in mRetina and in hfRPE. There are several striking differences. Lactate and succinate are more abundant in mRetina than in hfRPE
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Citrate and α-ketoglutarate are more abundant in hfRPE than in mRetina
source: whereas citrate and α-ketoglutarate are more abundant in hfRPE than in mRetina.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Decarboxylation of pyruvate predominates in mRetina, whereas carboxylation is more prominent in hfRPE
source: Figure 3C shows that decarboxylation of pyruvate predominates in mRetina, whereas carboxylation is more prominent in hfRPE.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data from U-13C glucose labeling shown in Figure 3C

claim: The lactate/citrate ratio in the mouse retina is nearly 30 times higher than in the mouse eyecup
source: Figure 4A compares the ratio of total lactate to total citrate in the retina vs. in the eyecup. Similar to the comparison of the lactate/citrate ratio for mouse retina vs. hfRPE, the lactate/citrate ratio in the mouse retina is nearly 30 times higher than in the mouse eyecup.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Retina releases 13C lactate into the medium ~20 times faster than either hfRPE or mEC
source: Retina releases 13C lactate into the medium ~20 times faster than either hfRPE or mEC.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 4B

claim: 13C from lactate accumulates in citrate pools at least 20 times faster than 13C from glucose in hfRPE cells
source: Figure 5A shows that 13C incorporates rapidly into the pyruvate pool from both 13C glucose and 13C lactate. However, in the citrate pools, 13C from lactate accumulates at least 20 times faster than 13C from glucose.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Substantial amounts of m3 malate form in hfRPE, indicating that carboxylation of pyruvate is a significant metabolic pathway
source: We also noted that substantial amounts of m3 malate form, indicating that carboxylation of pyruvate is a significant metabolic pathway in hfRPE.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 5A

claim: 13C lactate metabolism in hfRPE is more similar to mEC metabolism than to retina metabolism
source: Figure 6 shows that 13C lactate metabolism in hfRPE is more similar to mEC metabolism than to retina metabolism.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data comparing metabolite distributions shown in Figure 6

claim: Lactate in the medium substantially increases NADH fluorescence in hfRPE cells
source: Figure 7B shows that lactate in the medium substantially increases NADH fluorescence, whereas pyruvate drives it to its oxidized state.
evidence: Supported by live-cell NADH fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Unlabeled lactate increases unlabeled pyruvate, citrate, isocitrate, fumarate and malate in hfRPE cells
source: Figure 7C shows that unlabeled lactate increases unlabeled pyruvate, citrate, isocitrate, fumarate and malate (left panel).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Addition of unlabeled lactate causes accumulation of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP)
source: Addition of unlabeled lactate also causes accumulation of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP), the triose phosphate immediately upstream of the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) reaction, a reaction that requires NAD+.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Lactate diminishes incorporation of 13C from U-13C glucose into intermediates downstream of the GAPDH reaction
source: Consistent with suppression of GAPDH activity, lactate diminishes incorporation of 13C from U-13C glucose into intermediates downstream of the GAPDH reaction (right panel of Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Exogenous lactate can suppress glycolysis in hfRPE cells
source: We conclude that exogenous lactate can suppress glycolysis in hfRPE cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including NADH fluorescence and metabolite labeling data

claim: 10 mM lactate causes similar suppression of glycolysis as 20 mM lactate
source: We also tested the effect of 10 mM lactate and found similar suppression of glycolysis, i.e. suppression of the formation of m3, but not m0 glycolytic intermediates (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 8A,B

claim: Both lactate and pyruvate suppress accumulation of 13C lactate in the medium
source: Figure 8G shows both lactate and pyruvate suppress accumulation of 13C lactate in the medium whereas alanine enhances it.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 8G

claim: Unlabeled lactate added to the apical medium substantially increases the accumulation of 13C glucose on the apical side of hfRPE monolayers
source: Figure 9B and C show that unlabeled lactate added to the apical medium substantially increases the accumulation of 13C glucose on the apical side.
evidence: Supported by transwell transport experiments shown in Figure 9B and C

claim: The effect of lactate on glucose transport is more pronounced when 2 mM instead of 5 mM 13C Glc is used
source: The effect of lactate is more pronounced when 2 mM (Panel F) instead of 5 mM 13C Glc (Panel E) is used, consistent with lactate suppressing consumption of glucose by the RPE.
evidence: Supported by transwell transport experiments shown in Figure 9B and C

claim: Unlabeled lactate in the apical compartment suppresses accumulation of 13C Pyr and 13C Lac on the apical side
source: Unlabeled lactate in the apical compartment also suppresses accumulation of 13C Pyr and 13C Lac on the apical side (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: Supported by transwell transport experiments shown in Figure 9B and C

claim: Pyruvate is released from mouse retinas at only 6.7 ± 2.3% of the rate of lactate release
source: In separate experiments with mouse retinas we found that pyruvate is released from mouse retinas at only 6.7 ± 2.3% of the rate of lactate release
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from mouse retinas

claim: Alanine is released from mouse retinas at only 0.4 ± 0.1% of the rate of lactate release
source: and alanine is released at only 0.4 ± 0.1% of that rate (StDev, n = 13).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from mouse retinas

claim: PKM2 is highly enriched in photoreceptors
source: The M2 isoform of PK (PKM2) is highly enriched in photoreceptors (Lindsay et al., 2014; Chinchore et al., 2017; Rajala et al., 2016; Rueda et al., 2016; Casson et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: MGCs in mouse retinas do not express substantial amounts of any PK isoform
source: but MGCs in mouse retinas do not express substantial amounts of any PK isoform (Lindsay et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindsay et al., 2014

claim: MGCs do not express hexokinase
source: MGCs also do not express hexokinase (Rueda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rueda et al., 2016

claim: Lactate, rather than glucose, is the most effective source of carbon for glutamine synthesis by MGCs in mouse retinas
source: Furthermore, lactate, rather than glucose, is the most effective source (Lindsay et al., 2014) of carbon for glutamine synthesis by MGCs (Riepe and Norenburg, 1977) in mouse retinas.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindsay et al., 2014 and Riepe and Norenburg, 1977

claim: Enhancing glycolysis delayed degeneration of photoreceptors in retinas where rods were degenerating as a consequence of a mutation associated with retinitis pigmentosa
source: Both found that making photoreceptors more glycolytic also makes them more robust. Enhancing glycolysis delayed degeneration of photoreceptors in retinas where rods were degenerating as a consequence of a mutation associated with retinitis pigmentosa (Zhang et al., 2016; Venkatesh et al., 2015).

claim: Making RPE cells more glycolytic in vivo causes neighboring photoreceptors to degenerate

source: When glycolysis in the RPE was enhanced by knocking out VHL (Kurihara et al., 2016) or by knocking out an essential mitochondrial transcription factor in RPE cells in vivo (Zhao et al., 2011) the neighboring photoreceptors died.

claim: RPE cells are specialized for a type of energy metabolism called reductive carboxylation
source: Recently, we showed that RPE cells are specialized for a type of energy metabolism called reductive carboxylation (Du et al., 2016b) that can support redox homeostasis.

claim: Retinas and tumors were two of the tissues identified in the 1920's by Warburg and Krebs as relying mostly on 'aerobic glycolysis'
source: Retinas and tumors were two of the tissues identified in the 1920's by Warburg and Krebs (Krebs, 1927; Warburg et al., 1924) as relying mostly on 'aerobic glycolysis'.
evidence: Supported by citations to Krebs, 1927 and Warburg et al., 1924

claim: Evidence indicates photoreceptors in the outer retina are the site of aerobic glycolysis
source: Evidence indicates photoreceptors in the outer retina are the site of aerobic glycolysis (Du et al., 2016a; Lindsay et al., 2014; Chinchore et al., 2017; Medrano and Fox, 1995; Wang et al., 1997; Winkler, 1981).

claim: The RPE is a monolayer of polarized cells between the choroid and retina that functions as a blood-retina barrier
source: The RPE is a monolayer of polarized cells between the choroid and retina that functions as a blood-retina barrier.

claim: Cells in the RPE, bound together by tight junctions, express specific transporter proteins on their basolateral and apical surfaces
source: Cells in the RPE, bound together by tight junctions, express specific transporter proteins on their basolateral and apical surfaces (Lehmann et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lehmann et al., 2014

claim: Glucose from the choroid passes through transporters on the basolateral surface of RPE cells
source: Glucose from the choroid passes through transporters on the basolateral surface and then wends its way through the cytoplasm of the RPE cell.

claim: The protein immunoreactive with the GLUT1 antibody is membrane associated
source: The protein immunoreactive with the GLUT1 antibody was confirmed to be membrane associated (Figure 1B).

claim: Rod inner segments are identified by the unique morphology of their mitochondria
source: Rod inner segments are identified by the unique morphology of their mitochondria labeled with mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase one antibody (MT-COX1).

claim: Rod mitochondria extend beyond the ends of the Müller glial cell apical processes
source: These mitochondria extend beyond the ends of the Müller glial cell (MGC) apical processes (Figure 1E).

claim: There are no mitochondria within the fine MGC apical processes
source: There are no mitochondria within these fine MGC apical processes.

claim: Small spherical-shaped mitochondria line up within the MGCs along the outer limiting membrane, just beneath the apical processes
source: Instead, small spherical-shaped mitochondria line up within the MGCs along the outer limiting membrane, just beneath the apical processes (Figure 1F and arrowheads in Figure 1C).

claim: MGCs extend from the outer limiting membrane to the ganglion cell side of the retina
source: MGCs, labeled with an antibody to glutamine synthetase (GS) in Figure 1D, extend from the outer limiting membrane to the ganglion cell side of the retina.

claim: Most GLUT1 immunoreactivity in MGCs is in the inner retina
source: Most GLUT1 immunoreactivity in MGCs is in the inner retina (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The distribution of GLUT1 immunoreactivity supports the idea that photoreceptors can take up glucose released from the apical side of the RPE
source: Taken altogether, the distribution of GLUT1 immunoreactivity supports the idea that photoreceptors can take up glucose released from the apical side of the RPE.

claim: The citrate and α-ketoglutarate pools are larger and fill more gradually in hfRPE cells than in retina
source: We also noted that the citrate and α-ketoglutarate pools are larger and fill more gradually in hfRPE cells than in retina indicating a large oxidative metabolic capacity of RPE mitochondria.

claim: Less than 2% of metabolic flux from glucose goes through the pentose phosphate pathway in both mRetina and hfRPE

claim: Metabolites with one 13C ('m1') are generated from glucose that flows through the oxidative reactions of the pentose phosphate pathway
source: Metabolites with one 13C ('m1') are generated from glucose that flows through the oxidative reactions of the pentose phosphate pathway

claim: Metabolites with two 13C ('m2') are produced when glucose enters glycolysis directly

source: Mitochondrial intermediates with two labeled carbons ('m2') are produced by decarboxylation of pyruvate
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of isotope labeling patterns in metabolic pathways

claim: Mitochondrial intermediates with three labeled carbons ('m3') are made by carboxylation of pyruvate
source: whereas those with three labeled carbons ('m3') are made by carboxylation of pyruvate.

claim: The hfRPE preparation has been widely used to study RPE metabolism and to model RPE-related diseases such as age-related macular degeneration
source: Due to its similarity to native RPE cells, this hfRPE preparation has been widely used to study RPE metabolism and to model RPE-related diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (Ablonczy et al., 2011; Adijanto and Philp, 2014; Blenkinsop et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2011; Sonoda et al., 2009).

claim: Lactate does not diminish incorporation of 13C from glucose into m2 citrate and m2 isocitrate
source: Lactate does not diminish incorporation of 13C from glucose into m2 citrate and m2 isocitrate.

claim: Enhanced TCA cycle activity may be caused by anaplerotic supplementation of unlabeled TCA cycle intermediates
source: This may reflect enhanced TCA cycle activity caused by anaplerotic supplementation of unlabeled TCA cycle intermediates (see left panel of Figure 7C).

claim: Pyruvate and its amino derivative, alanine, cause redistributions of the relative amounts of specific glycolytic and mitochondrial intermediates
source: Pyruvate and its amino derivative, alanine, cause redistributions of the relative amounts of specific glycolytic and mitochondrial intermediates (Figure 8C–F).

claim: The effect of pyruvate may be attributable to accumulation of cytosolic NAD+ accelerating GAPDH activity while at the same time inhibiting malate-aspartate shuttle activity
source: The effect of pyruvate may be attributable to accumulation of cytosolic NAD+ accelerating GAPDH activity while at the same time inhibiting malate-aspartate shuttle activity (Du et al., 2013a).

claim: Alanine raises the levels of glutamate and aspartate
source: Alanine raises the levels of glutamate and aspartate, which may counteract the effect of pyruvate, derived from the alanine, on the malate-aspartate shuttle.

claim: Lactate from photoreceptors suppresses glycolysis in the RPE so more glucose can reach the retina
source: We propose that lactate from photoreceptors suppresses glycolysis in the RPE so more glucose can reach the retina.

claim: MGCs are fueled by lactate from photoreceptors
source: Based on these observations, we proposed that MGCs in a retina are fueled by lactate from photoreceptors (Hurley et al., 2015).

claim: The central metabolic role of photoreceptors in retinal energy metabolism is to convert glucose to lactate, which then is distributed to both RPE and MGCs to be used as fuel
source: Altogether, those findings and the results described in this report, indicate that the central metabolic role of photoreceptors in retinal energy metabolism is to convert glucose to lactate, which then is distributed to both RPE and MGCs to be used as fuel (Figure 10).

claim: Enhanced capacity for anabolic metabolism has been proposed as the purpose of aerobic glycolysis in photoreceptors

source: We propose that the laminated structure of the eye, in which the RPE separates the retina from its source of nutrients, requires photoreceptors to produce and release lactate to fuel MGC's and suppress glycolysis in the RPE so that sufficient glucose can flow through the RPE.

claim: Loss of a cone viability factor that normally is produced by rods may contribute to cone degeneration when rods degenerate
source: One reason for this is that loss of a cone viability factor that normally is produced by rods may contribute to cone degeneration in this type of disease state (Aït-Ali et al., 2015).
